common_name: Sizzler Red Salvia (Dwarf Bedding Scarlet Sage)

planting.note: Start seed indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost since seedlings are slow early on, then harden off and set out only after nights stay reliably warm. Sizzler Red is one of the earliest-flowering dwarf salvia strains, so it colors up in packs well before taller bedding types.

directions: Sizzler Red is a dwarf, uniform selection bred for dense flower columns on a tight, mounded habit well suited to packs and small containers as well as mass bedding. Give it full sun and evenly moist, well-drained soil, and pinch or shear lightly after the first flush to encourage rebranching if plants stretch in hot weather. Regular feeding keeps the compact habit from thinning out over a long summer bloom season. It holds color well through heat and humidity, though afternoon shade helps flower quality in the hottest inland climates.

common_name: Sizzler Purple Salvia (Dwarf Bedding Scarlet Sage)

planting.note: Sow indoors 6-8 weeks ahead of the last frost and transplant once soil has warmed; deep violet-purple spikes appear earlier than on standard tall salvia strains. Avoid setting plants out too early, as cold soil stalls establishment.

directions: This compact series member produces rich purple flower spikes on a densely branched, uniform mound that stays tidy without deadheading. Plant in full sun and fertile, well-drained soil; consistent moisture during establishment produces the fullest flower count. Because the habit is naturally short, avoid high-nitrogen feeding that promotes leaf growth over flowering. It performs reliably in containers, edging, and mass plantings where a low, colorful border is wanted.

common_name: Sizzler Salmon Salvia (Dwarf Bedding Scarlet Sage)

planting.note: Start indoors under bright light 6-8 weeks before the last frost; the soft salmon-pink color is a useful alternative to typical scarlet salvia for mixed pastel plantings. Transplant only once frost danger has fully passed.

directions: Sizzler Salmon offers a softer, coral-pink flower spike on the same tight, early-flowering plant as the rest of the series, making it a good pastel companion for red or purple salvia in combination plantings. Grow in full sun with well-drained soil and steady watering; the compact habit tolerates light shearing if plants become uneven mid-season. It is more heat-tolerant than many pastel bedding annuals and continues blooming through summer with routine feeding. Watch for stretch in overly shaded or overcrowded plantings, which dulls the color display.

common_name: Sizzler Burgundy Halo Salvia (Dwarf Bicolor Bedding Scarlet Sage)

planting.note: Start seed indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost date; the bicolor burgundy-and-white flowers give this selection a distinct look among red-flowered bedding salvias. Transplant after soil has warmed and nights stay above 50°F.

directions: Burgundy Halo stands out from other Sizzler colors with a two-toned flower — deep wine-burgundy petals ringed with a pale halo — carried on the same compact, early-blooming plant. Grow in full sun and well-drained, moderately fertile soil, watering deeply but infrequently once plants are established. The tight habit needs little grooming, though removing spent spikes keeps new color coming later into the season. It combines well with silver-leaved companions that set off the unusual bicolor bloom.

common_name: Salsa Rose Salvia (Compact Bedding Scarlet Sage)

planting.note: Start indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost date and transplant once soil has warmed; Salsa Rose flowers earlier than older tall salvia strains, filling bedding displays quickly. Give young plants bright light to prevent stretching.

directions: Salsa Rose brings a clear rose-pink flower spike to this early, uniform bedding series, useful for softer color schemes than the more common scarlet salvias. Site in full sun to light afternoon shade in fertile, well-drained soil, and keep watering consistent while plants establish. The dense, well-branched habit fills beds and containers quickly and needs only occasional deadheading to keep flowering strong into fall. It tolerates summer heat and humidity better than many pastel bedding annuals.
sources: North Carolina State Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox

common_name: Salsa Scarlet Bicolor Salvia (Compact Bedding Scarlet Sage)

planting.note: Start seed indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost; the scarlet-and-white bicolor spikes make this selection a distinctive accent among solid-red bedding salvias. Move outdoors only after nights stay reliably warm.

directions: This bicolor Salsa selection layers bright scarlet over white on each individual floret, giving flower spikes a lively, textured look rather than a flat block of color. Grow in full sun with well-drained, moderately fertile soil and consistent moisture, especially while plants are filling in. Its compact, well-branched habit suits both bedding rows and mixed containers, and light deadheading extends the display into autumn. It handles heat and summer humidity as well as any of the classic scarlet sages.

common_name: Salsa Light Purple Salvia (Compact Bedding Scarlet Sage)

planting.note: Start indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost date and transplant after danger of frost has passed; the soft lavender-purple flower spikes pair well with silver or white companion plants in mixed beds.

directions: Salsa Light Purple carries pale lavender-violet spikes on the same early, compact framework as the rest of the Salsa series, offering a gentler alternative to the traditional red bedding salvia. Plant in full sun to part shade in well-drained soil, watering deeply during dry spells once roots are established. Its tidy, well-filled habit needs minimal pinching and holds its shape through a long summer bloom period. Combine it with warm-toned annuals for contrast or with white flowers for a cooler palette.

common_name: Salsa Salmon Bicolor Salvia (Compact Bedding Scarlet Sage)

planting.note: Sow indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost; the soft salmon-and-cream bicolor flowers give this Salsa selection a muted, cottage-garden feel uncommon among bedding salvias. Transplant once soil has warmed.

directions: This two-toned Salsa cultivar mixes soft salmon with a pale cream base on each flower, producing a muted effect rather than the usual bold scarlet of bedding salvia. Site in full sun to light afternoon shade with fertile, well-drained soil and water regularly through the establishment period. The compact, early-flowering habit fills beds and pots quickly and rebounds well after occasional shearing. It is a good choice for gardeners wanting a hummingbird-friendly salvia in a softer color range.

planting.note: Start seed indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost date and set plants out once the soil is warm; Cleopatra is a compact, free-flowering strain suited to bedding rows and mass plantings.

directions: Cleopatra produces the classic dense scarlet flower spikes of bedding salvia on a well-branched, moderately compact plant that fills space faster than older tall strains. Grow in full sun in fertile, well-drained soil, keeping moisture consistent while the root system establishes. It benefits from occasional deadheading of finished spikes to keep new flower columns forming through summer. Heat and humidity tolerance are good, making it a dependable choice for long, hot growing seasons.

common_name: Cleopatra White Salvia (Compact White Bedding Sage)

planting.note: Start indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost and transplant after all frost danger has passed; clean white spikes make this a useful moon-garden or accent selection among the mostly red-flowered splendens cultivars.

directions: Cleopatra White departs from the typical scarlet sage palette with pure white flower spikes on an upright, easy-care plant that fits well into evening or all-white garden schemes. Plant in full sun to light afternoon shade in well-drained soil, and expect good drought tolerance once roots are established. Deadhead spent spikes periodically to keep the plant flowering steadily from early summer into fall. It combines effectively with darker-flowered annuals for strong visual contrast in beds, borders, and large containers.

planting.note: Sow indoors 8-10 weeks before the last frost, since this taller heirloom-type strain needs a longer season than modern dwarf series, and transplant once nights stay reliably warm. It rewards a full growing season with long, showy flower spikes.

directions: Bonfire is an old-fashioned, taller-growing scarlet sage prized for its long, densely packed spikes of vivid red flowers that keep coming from midsummer clear through the first hard frost. Plant in full sun to light shade in fertile, well-drained soil, and water regularly during establishment, tapering off once plants are rooted in. The upright, slightly bushy habit benefits from staking in windy sites but otherwise needs little maintenance beyond occasional deadheading. Its heat and humidity tolerance make it a dependable performer in long, hot summers, and hummingbirds visit it readily.

common_name: Forest Fire Salvia (Compact Red Tropical Sage)

planting.note: Direct sow or set out transplants after all danger of frost has passed; Forest Fire is part of the Hummingbird strain of tropical sage and flowers over an unusually long season on a compact, well-branched plant.

directions: Forest Fire is a compact, bushy selection of tropical sage bearing loose spikes of brilliant fire-red flowers set off by near-black calyxes, a small but distinctive detail that separates it from plain-red seed strains. Grow in full sun to light shade in lean, well-drained soil — rich soil produces excess foliage at the expense of bloom. It is heat, humidity, and drought tolerant once established and needs only occasional watering during prolonged dry spells. Hummingbirds and butterflies visit it readily, and it self-seeds freely in warm climates, often naturalizing where it is grown for more than one season.

common_name: Summer Jewel White Salvia (Compact White Tropical Sage)

planting.note: Direct sow or transplant after frost danger has passed; this 2015 All-America Selections winner flowers roughly two weeks earlier than comparable white salvias and stays compact for beds and containers alike.

directions: Summer Jewel White brings a clean white counterpart to the popular red and pink members of this compact tropical sage series, with the same early, prolific flowering on whorled spikes above upright, well-branched plants. Site in full sun to partial shade in lean, well-drained soil; established plants tolerate drought and rebound quickly after storms or heavy rain. Deadheading is not required for continued bloom, though removing early spikes can encourage even fuller flowering later in the season. It draws bees, butterflies, and hummingbirds and pairs well with the red and pink Summer Jewel colors for a mixed pollinator planting.
